subject: Private deploy: key custody, operator service account limits, and DPA redlines
messages:
From: Marta Ruiz <marta.ruiz@acmehealth.com>
To: jordan_blake@redwood.example.com
Cc: procurement@acmehealth.com, eng@acmehealth.com
Date: Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:12:00 -0800
Subject: Questions on private deployment key custody and operator access

Jordan,

Thanks for the demo earlier. Legal and infra dug into the private deployment proposal and we have a few open items before we can sign:

1) Key custody: we see a couple of options in the draft — customer-managed KMS, escrow with vendor, or vendor-held keys. Acme cannot accept vendor-held keystores. Our preferred model is BYOK where keys live in our cloud account. Can you confirm the exact handoff pattern you support for BYOK? We need to understand operator access in emergency situations.

2) Service accounts / operator access: the DPA redlines ask that operator accounts have no ability to retrieve plaintext customer data or unencrypted model inputs/outputs. We need a clear assurance of separation of duties and an auditable ephemeral access mechanism for break-glass situations.

3) Subprocessors & transfers: please send the current subprocessors list for the private deploy control plane and confirmation of whether any telemetry or logs containing PII could cross borders.

Attached are our DPA redlines (DPA_Acme_redlines.pdf). Please let us know whether Redwood can accept the language or propose alternative text.

Best,
Marta Ruiz
Sr. Counsel, Acme Health
(attachment: DPA_Acme_redlines.pdf)
From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.example.com>
To: Marta Ruiz <marta.ruiz@acmehealth.com>
Cc: irene_choi@redwood.example.com, kimberly_park@redwood.example.com
Date: Sat, 21 Nov 2026 09:03:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Questions on private deployment key custody and operator access

Marta — thanks, and really appreciate the clear asks. Short answers up front, followed by a proposed operational pattern and next steps.

1) BYOK handoff: yes — we support a customer-managed KMS hosted in your cloud account (AWS KMS / Azure Key Vault / GCP KMS). The recommended pattern is: customer creates CMK, grants Redwood a restricted asymmetric-encrypt-only key-wrapping grant (no decrypt permission), and we store only the key-wrapping key reference. For signing / decrypt operations used by the runtime, we perform them by calling a customer-side agent running in your VPC that holds the actual decrypt permission (agent communicates over mTLS to the runtime).

2) Operator access / break-glass: we do not store keys, and operator service accounts cannot request raw key material. For emergencies we propose an escalation flow:
  - Emergency approval requires two-party approval from your security contact + your delegated on-call (via a signed ticket in your tracking system).
  - If approved, we can request a short-lived, narrowly scoped STS token in your account that permits a small set of operator actions (e.g., push a hotfix image, collect runtime metadata). All actions are logged to your account logs and to Redwood audit events.
  - We can add a technical guard that blocks API calls that would surface plaintext model inputs/outputs unless a specific, time-limited flag is enabled and a request id is recorded.

3) Subprocessors & telemetry: current control plane subprocessors are: AWS (control plane hosting), Fastly (CDN for the console), and PagerDuty (alerts). For private deployments we can avoid cross-border telemetry by routing logs to your VPC; any telemetry we receive is configurable and by default redacted of PII. We will provide the full subprocessors appendix and a commitment to notify you 30 days prior to onboarding additional subprocessors.

Irene, can you sketch the exact network/auth pattern (agent + key grants + audit path) we should propose back to Acme? Kimberly — can you confirm whether the DPA redlines on key escrow (they want to strike vendor-escrow) are acceptable operationally?

I'll follow up with a proposed DPA paragraph and a diagram to attach.

— Jordan

Jordan Blake
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.example.com>
To: jordan_blake@redwood.example.com
Cc: kimberly_park@redwood.example.com, marta.ruiz@acmehealth.com
Date: Sun, 21 Nov 2026 12:18:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Questions on private deployment key custody and operator access

Folks — adding the technical sketch below so Acme has something concrete to review. I've attached a simple diagram (privdep-access-diagram.png).

Technical sketch (high level):

- Components: Customer VPC (KMS, runtime agent, logging collector) <--> Private runtime (Redwood-managed nodes in customer VPC or on-prem) <--> Redwood control plane (no key material).

- Key flow: Customer creates CMK with Decrypt disabled for any Redwood-managed principal. Instead:
  * Customer deploys a small runtime agent (docker) into a secured subnet; the agent holds an IAM role that can call KMS:Decrypt for that CMK.
  * The Redwood runtime communicates with the agent over mTLS using mutual certs tied to the deployment id. The runtime requests the agent to unwrap session keys; the agent performs KMS:Decrypt inside the customer's account and returns ephemeral session keys that are memory-only and rotated per-request.
  * Redwood never stores unwrapped keys at rest. Only ephemeral in-memory caches (KV cache) with TTL and strict zero-swap policies.

- Operator/service account constraints:
  * Redwood operator accounts are limited to orchestration metadata (pod status, node health) and cannot call the agent or KMS directly.
  * Any operator action that elevates privileges triggers an automated ticket and requires two approvers from ACME's side to issue a signed approval token.
  * All operator actions and agent responses are logged into the customer's logging collector (CloudWatch/StackDriver) and a Redwood audit stream. Logs containing model I/O are redacted at the agent before export.

- Telemetry & cross-border:
  * By default all telemetry stays in the customer's region. We support a local-only mode: Redwood control plane receives metadata hashes only (no raw I/O) and full traces are pushed to your S3/GCS bucket under your account.

Open questions for legal: what level of procedural detail do you want codified in the DPA vs. operational runbooks?

Irene
Principal Infra Engineer, Redwood Inference
(attachment: privdep-access-diagram.png)
From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.example.com>
To: Marta Ruiz <marta.ruiz@acmehealth.com>, procurement@acmehealth.com
Cc: irene_choi@redwood.example.com, kimberly_park@redwood.example.com
Date: Mon, 22 Nov 2026 09:03:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Questions on private deployment key custody and operator access

Marta / Alex — attaching the DPA paragraph we recommend plus the diagram. Summary of proposed DPA language highlights (we can insert as an annex):

- Key custody: Redwood will not hold, transport, or escrow customer key material. Customer-held keys (BYOK) are required for production private deployments. The contract will require Redwood to accept a key-wrapping-only grant and to operate the in-VPC agent pattern described earlier.

- Operator access: Redwood will restrict operator roles so they cannot retrieve plaintext customer data or call KMS directly. Emergency operator actions require a documented two-party approval from the customer's security contact and an on-call approver; any such action must be logged and the logs retained for 24 months.

- Subprocessors & notice: For private deployments, Redwood will limit external subprocessors that can access any customer metadata to those listed in Annex B. Redwood will provide 30 days notice of additions and will offer reasonable alternatives (e.g., self-hosted integrations) where feasible.

- Audit & evidence: Redwood will provide (a) architecture diagrams and runbooks, (b) sample audit logs from a staging deployment, and (c) a SOC-like questionnaire focused on operational controls for private deployments.

If this approach is acceptable, we suggest:
  - Legal aligns on the annex wording (I reworded a couple of your redline bullet points to match the technical flow).
  - Acme infra (Ravi) signs off on the agent pattern and provides a sample IAM role template.
  - Contract team routes the redlines to Kimberly for final language and an addendum.

Next steps: Kimberly — can you please review the attached proposed paragraph and confirm if legal/commercial can accept (or propose minimal alternative language) by Tue EOD? Marta / Alex — if you prefer, we can set a short 30-minute call to walk through the diagram.

Thanks — Jordan

Jordan Blake
Senior Sales Engineer, Redwood Inference
